claim: The emergence of symbolic thinking has been proposed as a dominant cognitive criterion to distinguish humans from other primates during hominisation.
source: The emergence of symbolic thinking has been proposed as a dominant cognitive criterion to distinguish humans from other primates during hominisation.
evidence: This is a statement about what has been proposed in the literature, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: One of the simplest features of a symbol is bidirectional attachment: the content is accessible from the symbol, and vice versa.
source: Although the proper definition of a symbol has been the subject of much debate, one of its simplest features is bidirectional attachment: the content is accessible from the symbol, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a definitional claim about symbols based on established understanding in the field.

claim: Non-human primates fail to generalise an association learned in one temporal order (A to B) to the reverse order (B to A).
source: Behavioural observations scattered over the past four decades suggest that this criterion might not be met in non-human primates, as they fail to generalise an association learned in one temporal order (A to B) to the reverse order (B to A).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to behavioral observations from prior research.

claim: After learning a unidirectional association, humans showed surprise signals when this learned association was violated.
source: After learning a unidirectional association, humans showed surprise signals when this learned association was violated.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: In humans, surprise signals to violated associations occurred spontaneously in both learned and reversed directions.
source: Crucially, this effect occurred spontaneously in both learned and reversed directions, within an extended network of high-level brain areas, including, but also going beyond, the language network.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the fMRI data.

claim: In humans, violations of association effects occurred within an extended network of high-level brain areas, including, but also going beyond, the language network.
source: Crucially, this effect occurred spontaneously in both learned and reversed directions, within an extended network of high-level brain areas, including, but also going beyond, the language network.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In monkeys, violations of association effects occurred solely in the learned direction.
source: In monkeys, by contrast, violations of association effects occurred solely in the learned direction and were largely confined to sensory areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI experiments.

claim: In monkeys, violations of association effects were largely confined to sensory areas.
source: In monkeys, by contrast, violations of association effects occurred solely in the learned direction and were largely confined to sensory areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI experiments.

claim: A human-specific brain network may have evolved the capacity for reversible symbolic reference.
source: We propose that a human-specific brain network may have evolved the capacity for reversible symbolic reference.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Symbols are ubiquitous in many domains of human cognition, underlying not only language but also mathematical, musical, or social representations.
source: Symbols are ubiquitous in many domains of human cognition, underlying not only language but also mathematical, musical, or social representations and many others domains (Deacon, 1998; Dehaene et al., 2022; Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019; Nieder, 2009; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The appearance of symbolic representations has been suggested as a potential marker signalling hominisation.
source: The appearance of symbolic representations, which would develop in parallel with the expansion of prefrontal and parietal associative areas, has therefore been suggested as a potential marker signalling hominisation (Deacon, 1998; Dehaene et al., 2022; Henshilwood et al., 2002; Neubauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many non-human animals, including chimpanzees, macaques, and dogs, are able to learn hundreds of indexical relationships, even with arbitrary signs.
source: In that respect, however, many non-human animals, including chimpanzees, macaques, but also dogs, are able to learn hundreds of such indexical relationships, even with arbitrary signs (Kaminski et al., 2004; Livingstone et al., 2010; Matsuzawa, 1985; Premack, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Bees can learn to associate arbitrary visual shapes to abstract representations such as visual quantities (two or three elements) independently of the density, size, and colour of the elements in the visual display.
source: Even bees can learn to associate arbitrary visual shapes to abstract representations such as visual quantities (two or three elements) independently of the density, size, and colour of the elements in the visual display (Howard et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Non-human animals' capacities for novel symbolic composition, especially of a recursive syntactic nature, appear limited or absent.
source: Non-human animals may be conditioned to acquire iconic or indexical associations (i.e. signs which bear, respectively, a non-arbitrary or arbitrary relationships between the signifier and the signified), and even perhaps perform operations on the learned signs, such as addition (Livingstone et al., 2014), but their capacities for novel symbolic composition, especially of a recursive syntactic nature, appear limited, or absent (Berwick and Chomsky, 2016; Dehaene et al., 2022; Dehaene et al., 2015; Penn et al., 2008; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021; Yang, 2013; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: While the associations between indices and objects are unidirectional, symbolic associations are bidirectional or symmetric.
source: While the associations between indices and objects (such as those acquired during classical conditioning) are unidirectional, as in the famous example of the bell indicating the food, symbolic associations are bidirectional or symmetric (Deacon, 1998; Nieder, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Non-human animals such as bees, pigeons, macaques, baboons, and chimpanzees struggle to reverse the associations that they learned in one direction.
source: A small number of behavioural studies, spread over four decades, report that non-human animals such as bees and pigeons, but also macaques, baboons, and chimpanzees, struggle to reverse the associations that they learned in one direction (Imai et al., 2021; Kojima, 1984; Lipkens et al., 1988; Medam et al., 2016; Sidman et al., 1982; Howard et al., 2019; see Chartier and Fagot, 2023, for a review and discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior behavioral research.

claim: In a recent experiment with 20 free-behaving baboons, after learning to pair visual shapes above 80% success, their performance dropped considerably when the order of presentation was subsequently reversed (54% correct, chance = 50%).
source: In a recent experiment, Chartier and Fagot, 2023 explored this question in 20 free-behaving baboons. After having learned to pair visual shapes (two pairs A–B) above 80% success, their performance dropped considerably when the order of presentation was subsequently reversed (B–A; 54% correct, chance = 50%), although their relearning performance was only slightly but significantly better when the reversed pairs were congruent (B1–A1; B2–A2) rather than incongruent (B1–A2; B2–A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Chimpanzee AI's capacity to associate signs and their meanings was based on an explicit and sequential training in both directions, at least initially.
source: Even for the famous case of chimpanzee AI, who learned Arabic numerals and other arbitrary tokens for colours and objects (Matsuzawa, 2009; Matsuzawa, 1985), it turns out that her capacity to associate signs and their meanings was based on an explicit and sequential training in both directions, at least initially (Kojima, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Humans as young as 8 months show behavioural evidence of immediate spontaneous reversal of learned associations.
source: In sharp contrast, humans as young as 8 months, even when tested under the same conditions as monkeys or baboons (Sidman et al., 1982), show behavioural evidence of immediate spontaneous reversal of learned associations (Imai et al., 2021; Ogawa et al., 2010; Sidman et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A recent EEG study with 4- to 5-month-old human infants showed violation-of-expectation responses in both canonical and reverse order.
source: A recent study from our lab used EEG to apply this approach to 4- to 5-month-old human infants (Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019). The infants were trained with pairs of stimuli in which a specific picture (a lion or a fish) was associated with tri-syllabic none words, depending on a rule concerning syllable-repetition in the word (e.g. xxY words such as babagu and didito were followed by the fish picture whereas xYx words such as lotilo and fudafu were followed by the lion picture). Violation-of-expectation responses were recorded in both canonical and reverse order, suggesting that preverbal human infants already have the ability to reversibly attach a symbol to an abstract rule.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Preverbal human infants already have the ability to reversibly attach a symbol to an abstract rule.
source: Violation-of-expectation responses were recorded in both canonical and reverse order, suggesting that preverbal human infants already have the ability to reversibly attach a symbol to an abstract rule.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the EEG study results cited.

claim: In human adults, an fMRI study with abstract patterns showed brain signatures suggestive of spontaneous reversal of learned associations.
source: In human adults, an fMRI study with a more complex design using explicit reports on associations between abstract patterns also showed brain signatures suggestive of spontaneous reversal of learned associations (Ogawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The network of brain areas showing spontaneous reversal in human adults overlapped with the multiple-demand system that is ubiquitously observed in high-level cognitive tasks.
source: The network of brain areas overlapped with the multiple-demand system that is ubiquitously observed in high-level cognitive tasks (Duncan, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2013), including bilateral inferior and middle frontal gyrus (IFG and MFG), anterior insula (AI), intra-parietal sulcus (IPS), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A human fMRI study investigating association learning between two natural visual objects found that violation effects in the learned direction were restricted to low-level visual areas.
source: In contrast, a human fMRI study investigating association learning between two natural visual objects found that violation effects in the learned direction were restricted to low-level visual areas (Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: In macaque monkeys, violation effects in the learned direction have been found selectively in visual areas, using fMRI as well as single-neuron recordings.
source: Similarly, in macaque monkeys violation effects in the learned direction have been found selectively in visual areas, using fMRI as well as single-neuron recordings (Kaposvari et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2014; Meyer and Olson, 2011; Vergnieux and Vogels, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A study testing whether learned associations spontaneously reversed in macaque monkeys showed no such reversal in a small subset of 17 neurons.
source: One of these studies (Meyer and Olson, 2011) also tested, in a small subset of 17 neurons, whether the learned associations spontaneously reversed, and showed no such reversal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: In experiment 1, humans (n = 31) and macaque monkeys (n = 2) were exposed to four pairs of visual objects and speech sounds over the course of 3 days.
source: Over the course of 3 days, we exposed humans (n = 31) and macaque monkeys (n = 2) to four pairs of visual objects and speech sounds (Figure 1A; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for the five series of four pairs of audio–visual stimuli).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample sizes.

claim: Two of the pairs were presented in the auditory-to-visual direction and two in the visual-to-auditory direction.
source: Two of the pairs were presented in the auditory-to-visual direction and two in the visual-to-auditory direction, ensuring that all subjects had experience with both orders and would not be surprised by their temporal reversal per se (see discussion of the utility of this point in Medam et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: After 3 consecutive days of exposure to 100% of congruent canonical trials, subjects were tested for learning using 3T fMRI.
source: After 3 consecutive days of exposure to 100% of congruent canonical trials (24 canonical trials in total per pair, presented outside the scanner), subjects were tested for learning using 3T fMRI, during which they were passively exposed to pairs that respected or violated the learned pairings (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The design included 70% of congruent canonical trials, 10% of incongruent canonical trials, 10% of reversed congruent trials, and 10% of reversed incongruent trials.
source: To sustain the memory for learned pairs, the design still included 70% of congruent canonical trials (identical to the trials to which they have been exposed outside the scanner). In addition, there were 10% of incongruent canonical trials, in which the temporal order was maintained but the pairings between auditory and visual stimuli were violated. Enhanced brain responses to such incongruent pairs would indicate surprise and therefore prove that the associations had been learned. Note that all auditory and visual stimuli themselves were familiar: only their pairing was unusual. The design also included 10% of reversed congruent and 10% of reversed incongruent trials, in which the habitual (i.e. canonical) order of presentation of the pairs was reversed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Visual and auditory stimuli could be separated by their temporal offsets in the fMRI data.
source: Although each trial comprises auditory and visual stimuli, these could be separated by the temporal offsets.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B and 1C showing activation in sensory cortices.

claim: In the visual cortex, the response evoked by the pair arose earlier when the first stimulus of the pair was visual compared to when it was auditory.
source: In the visual cortex, the response evoked by the pair arose earlier when the first stimulus of the pair was visual compared to when it was auditory, and the other way around for the auditory cortex (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and 1E with hemodynamic response data.

claim: In the auditory cortex of monkeys the response was relatively weak.
source: In the auditory cortex of monkeys the response was relatively weak (Figure 1C, E), in line with previous studies (Erb et al., 2019; Petkov et al., 2009; Uhrig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and 1E and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The weak auditory cortex response in monkeys might be related to the small size of auditory cortex relative to visual cortex in monkeys.
source: This might be related to the small size of auditory cortex relative to visual cortex in monkeys (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), as well as relative to the size of the human auditory cortex (Woods et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In humans, a vast network was activated by incongruity on both canonical and reversed trials.
source: Indeed, in humans, a vast network was activated by incongruity on both canonical and reversed trials (voxel p < 0.001, cluster p < 0.05 corrected, n = 31 participants) (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: The network activated by incongruity in humans included bilateral IFG, MFG, AI, IPS, and dACC.
source: This network included a set of high-level brain regions previously described as the multiple-demand system (Duncan, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2013), including bilateral IFG, MFG, AI, IPS, and dACC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The network activated by incongruity in humans included the language network, with the left superior temporal sulcus (STS).
source: It also included the language network (Pallier et al., 2011), with the left superior temporal sulcus (STS), in addition to the left inferior frontal region already mentioned.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The activation in humans was bilateral, supporting the model that the language network is part of a larger symbolic network.
source: However, in our case the activation was bilateral, thereby supporting the model that the language network is part of a larger symbolic network (Dehaene et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bilateral activation pattern observed.

claim: In humans, activations were also found in the precuneus, similar to the network involved in top–down attention to memorised visual stimuli.
source: Furthermore, we also found activations in the precuneus, similar to the network that has been found for top–down attention to memorised visual stimuli (Sestieri et al., 2010), which also included bilateral STS and IPS.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In humans, no congruity effects were found in visually activated regions, in contrast to a previous human fMRI study.
source: Notably, we did not find any congruity effects in visually activated regions (compare to Figure 1B), in contrast to a previous human fMRI study (Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In humans, no significant cluster exhibited any interaction between congruity and canonicity.
source: However, no significant cluster exhibited any interaction between congruity and canonicity, indicating that there was no statistical difference between the effect of congruity for the trained and the reversed direction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The human brain fully and spontaneously reverses the auditory–visual associations that it learns.
source: Thus, the human brain fully and spontaneously reverses the auditory–visual associations that it learns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In monkeys, the canonical congruity effect was not significant when analysing the first imaging sessions after the first 3 days of exposure to the canonical pairs.
source: The canonical congruity effect, which indexes learning, was not significant when analysing the first imaging sessions (n = 5) after the first 3 days of exposure to the canonical pairs.
evidence: This is a finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: Monkeys were further exposed during 2 weeks for three of the five stimulus sets (with in total ~960 canonical trials per pair) and tested during 4 consecutive days.
source: As we had anticipated this based on previous work (Meyer and Olson, 2011), monkeys were further exposed during 2 weeks for three of the five stimulus sets (with in total ~960 canonical trials per pair) and tested during 4 consecutive days.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for monkeys.

claim: After extended exposure, consistent effects were found in both monkeys, with clusters in early visual areas (V1, V2, and V4), and auditory association areas in the left temporo-parieto-occipital cortex.
source: After this extended exposure, we found consistent effects in both monkeys (averaged over the 12 scan sessions, 4 per stimulus set per monkey), with clusters in early visual areas (V1, V2, and V4), and auditory association areas in the left temporo-parieto-occipital cortex (AV and VA trials combined, p < 0.001, cluster p < 0.05, n = 2) (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: In monkeys, the congruity effect was confined to the canonical direction, with no significant clusters in the reversed direction at the whole-brain level.
source: Crucially, however, this effect was confined to the canonical direction, with no significant clusters in the reversed direction at the whole-brain level, in accordance with the reversibility hypothesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In monkeys, the interaction effect between congruity and canonicity showed an activation pattern similar to the canonical congruity effect, which reached significance in areas V2 and V4.
source: We specifically tested the difference between the congruity effect in the learned and the reversed direction by calculating the interaction effect between congruity and canonicity, which showed an activation pattern that was similar to the canonical congruity effect, which reached significance in areas V2 and V4.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: Monkey cortex could acquire audio–visual pairings, but with two major differences with humans: the congruity effects did not involve a broad network of high-level cortical areas but remained restricted to early sensory areas, and the learned associations did not reverse.
source: The results thus indicated that monkey cortex could acquire audio–visual pairings, as also shown by prior visual–visual experiments (Meyer and Olson, 2011; Vergnieux and Vogels, 2020), but with two major differences with humans: the congruity effects did not involve a broad network of high-level cortical areas but remained restricted to early sensory areas, and the learned associations did not reverse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, a reward association was introduced to promote monkeys' engagement in the task.
source: In experiment 2, a reward association was introduced to promote monkeys' engagement in the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, within each presentation direction, one of the two pictures of objects was associated with a high reward, and one with a low reward.
source: Within each presentation direction, one of the two pictures of objects was associated with a high reward, and one with a low reward (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, significant canonical congruity effects were obtained in monkeys on the first imaging day after the initial training (24 trials per pair).
source: Using this design, we obtained significant canonical congruity effects in monkeys on the first imaging day after the initial training (24 trials per pair), indicating that the animals had learned the associations (Figure 4B and Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4B and Table 3.

claim: In experiment 2, the congruity effect in monkeys was found in visual areas (V1, V2, and V4), also spreading to the prefrontal cortex (45B and 46v).
source: The effect was again found in visual areas (V1, V2, and V4), also spreading to the prefrontal cortex (45B and 46v), very similar to the visually activated areas (compare to Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, small clusters were also found in area 6 and in STS in monkeys.
source: In addition, small clusters were also found in area 6 and in STS.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, the congruity effect in monkeys remained restricted to the learned direction, as no area showed a significant reversed congruity effect.
source: Crucially, the congruity effect remained restricted to the learned direction, as no area showed a significant reversed congruity effect, again in accordance with the reversibility hypothesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, the interaction between congruity and canonicity in monkeys indicated that there was a significant difference between the canonical and the reversed direction in a similar set of regions (V1, V2, area 45A, 46v, and 6).
source: The interaction between congruity and canonicity indicated that there was a significant difference between the canonical and the reversed direction in a similar set of regions (V1, V2, area 45A, 46v, and 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: The greater involvement of the frontal cortex in the congruity effect in experiment 2 fits with previous reports on the impact of reward association on long-term memory for visual stimuli in macaque monkeys.
source: The greater involvement of the frontal cortex in the congruity effect in this paradigm fits with previous reports on the impact of reward association on long-term memory for visual stimuli in macaque monkeys (Ghazizadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data and supported by a citation.

claim: In experiment 2, the congruity effect in monkeys was present only for high-reward conditions, with a significant interaction of congruity and reward in area 45 and caudate nucleus.
source: To further investigate this, we split high versus low rewarded pairs and found that congruity effect was present only for high-reward conditions, with a significant interaction of congruity and reward in area 45 and caudate nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the monkey fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Even when stimuli were optimised and made relevant for monkeys, leading to enhanced activations and an activation of prefrontal cortex to violations of expectations, the learned associations did not reverse in monkeys.
source: Overall, these results indicate that, even when stimuli were optimised and made relevant for monkeys, leading to enhanced activations and an activation of prefrontal cortex to violations of expectations, the learned associations did not reverse in monkeys.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the monkey fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, humans again gave evidence of reversed association, although weaker than with spoken words.
source: We also ran this visual–visual paradigm in human participants (n = 24) with the goal to clarify the role of language in the reversibility process. Humans again gave evidence of reversed association, although weaker than with spoken words (Figure 4C and Table 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the human fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Table 4.

claim: In experiment 2, the main effect of congruity in humans was significant in a network very similar to experiment 1, including bilateral MFG, left IPS, bilateral AI, dACC, with an additional focus in left inferior temporal (IT) gyrus.
source: At the normal threshold (voxel p < 0.001, cluster p < 0.05 corrected), the main effect of congruity was significant in a network very similar to experiment 1, including bilateral MFG, left IPS, bilateral AI, dACC, with an additional focus in left inferior temporal (IT) gyrus (Figure 4C and Table 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the human fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Table 4.

claim: In experiment 2, the involvement of the language network in humans was limited, with a main effect of congruity in the STS being absent.
source: The involvement of the language network was limited. In particular a main effect of congruity in the STS was absent, in agreement with the shift to visual symbols.
evidence: This is a finding from the human fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, bilateral middle frontal gyri, STS, and the precuneus were activated by the incongruent minus congruent contrast on reversed trials in humans.
source: Still, bilateral middle frontal gyri, STS, and the precuneus were again activated by the incongruent minus congruent contrast on reversed trials (voxel p < 0.001, cluster p < 0.05 corrected), thereby extending beyond the multiple-demand system (Duncan, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the human fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, sensory activated regions were absent in humans, in contrast to a previous study on congruity effects when using associations between two visual objects.
source: While sensory activated regions were again absent, in contrast to a previous study on congruity effects in humans when using associations between two visual objects (Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the human fMRI data analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, no interaction effect was found between congruity and canonicity in humans, neither at the classical threshold (p < 0.001) nor at a lower threshold (p < 0.01).
source: And crucially, no interaction effect was again found between congruity and canonicity, neither at the classical threshold (p < 0.001) nor at a lower threshold (p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the human fMRI data analysis.

claim: Humans can encode pairs of visual stimuli in a symmetrical, reversible fashion, involving a network of high-level cortical areas, unlike monkeys.
source: Those results indicate that humans can also encode pairs of visual stimuli in a symmetrical, reversible fashion, involving a network of high-level cortical areas, unlike monkeys.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the human fMRI data analysis.

claim: In the joint analysis of both experiments, there was a main effect of experiment with greater activation in a bilateral auditory and linguistic network in the AV experiment, and in the occipital, occipito-temporal, and occipito-parietal visual pathways in the VV experiment.
source: There was, unsurprisingly, a main effect of experiment with greater activation in a bilateral auditory and linguistic network in the AV experiment, and in the occipital, occipito-temporal, and occipito-parietal visual pathways in the VV experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint analysis of both human experiments.

claim: In the joint analysis, a main effect of congruity was observed in bilateral regions: insula, MFG, precentral, IPS, precuneus, ACC, and STS.
source: A main effect of congruity was observed and was again significant in both directions, canonical and reversed, in bilateral regions: insula, MFG, precentral, IPS, precuneus, ACC, and STS.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint analysis of both human experiments.

claim: In the joint analysis, there was still no region sensitive to the congruity × canonicity interaction.
source: Crucially, there was still no region sensitive to the congruity × canonicity interaction, indicating that the learned associations were fully reversible.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint analysis of both human experiments.

claim: In the joint analysis, a single region, the left posterior STS, showed a significantly different congruity effect in the two experiments, as it was slightly larger in the AV relative to VV paradigm.
source: Finally, a single region, the left posterior STS, showed a significantly different congruity effect in the two experiments, as it was slightly larger in the AV relative to VV paradigm ([−60 –40 8], z = 4.51; 183 vox, pcor = 0.049), compatible with a specific role in learning of new spoken lexical items.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint analysis of both human experiments.

claim: A broad and bilateral network, encompassing language areas but extending beyond them into dorsal parietal and prefrontal cortices, responded to violations of reversible symbolic association regardless of modality.
source: The results therefore suggest that a broad and bilateral network, encompassing language areas but extending beyond them into dorsal parietal and prefrontal cortices, responded to violations of reversible symbolic association regardless of modality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the joint analysis of both human experiments.

claim: A main congruity effect was observed in all ROIs in the localiser analysis.
source: A main congruity effect was observed in all ROIs (Table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the ROI analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: In the ROI analysis, there was a main effect of experiment in all language ROIs, VWFA and right IT.
source: There was also a main effect of experiment in all language ROIs, VWFA and right IT, due on the one hand to larger activations in the AV than VV experiment in frontal and superior temporal ROIs, and on the other hand to the converse trend in the VWFA and IT ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: In the ROI analysis, a significant congruity × experiment interaction was seen only in the pSTS and IFG triangularis.
source: A significant congruity × experiment interaction was seen only in the pSTS and IFG triangularis, because these ROIs showed a large congruity effect in the AV experiment, but no effect in the VV experiment – thus further confirming that these areas contribute specifically to the acquisition of linguistic symbols, while all other areas were engaged regardless of modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: In the ROI analysis, no significant interaction canonicity × congruity nor experiment × canonicity × congruity were observed.
source: Importantly, in all these analyses, no significant interaction canonicity × congruity nor experiment × canonicity × congruity were observed, confirming the whole-brain analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, a within-subject behavioural index of reversibility was correlated with the fMRI congruity effect on canonical trials (r = 0.49, p = 0.028) and especially on reversed trials (r = 0.64, p = 0.002) in the left dorsal part of area 44.
source: Finally, in experiment 2 in which participants rated the familiarity of the pairs, we computed a within-subject behavioural index of reversibility as the difference in familiarity rating between incongruent and congruent reversed pairs. Across subjects, this index was correlated with the fMRI congruity effect (difference between incongruent and congruent trials in the ROI) on canonical trials (r = 0.49, p = 0.028) and especially on reversed trials (r = 0.64, p = 0.002) in the left dorsal part of area 44.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: In the right cerebellum, a correlation between the behavioral index of reversibility and the fMRI congruity effect was observed but only for the reversed trials (r = 0.57, p = 0.008).
source: In the right cerebellum, a similar correlation was observed but only for the reversed trials (r = 0.57, p = 0.008).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: Humans reported a higher familiarity with congruent canonical pairs than with congruent reversed pairs (t(20) = 2.8, p = 0.01).
source: Although participants reported a higher familiarity with congruent canonical pairs (which were presented on 70% of trials) than with congruent reversed pairs (which were presented on 10% of trials, t(20) = 2.8, p = 0.01), both pairs were rated as much more familiar than their corresponding incongruent pairs (although they were also presented 10% of time), and than never-seen pairs (all t(20) > 7, p < 0.0001, bilateral paired t-test).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral familiarity rating task.

claim: Both congruent canonical and congruent reversed pairs were rated as much more familiar than their corresponding incongruent pairs and than never-seen pairs (all t(20) > 7, p < 0.0001).
source: Although participants reported a higher familiarity with congruent canonical pairs (which were presented on 70% of trials) than with congruent reversed pairs (which were presented on 10% of trials, t(20) = 2.8, p = 0.01), both pairs were rated as much more familiar than their corresponding incongruent pairs (although they were also presented 10% of time), and than never-seen pairs (all t(20) > 7, p < 0.0001, bilateral paired t-test).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral familiarity rating task.

claim: The familiarity task confirms that humans spontaneously reverse associations and experience a memory illusion of seeing the reversed pairs.
source: This familiarity task thus confirms that humans spontaneously reverse associations and experience a memory illusion of seeing the reversed pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral familiarity rating task.

claim: Several studies previously found behavioural evidence for a uniquely human ability to spontaneously reverse a learned association.
source: Several studies previously found behavioural evidence for a uniquely human ability to spontaneously reverse a learned association (Imai et al., 2021; Kojima, 1984; Lipkens et al., 1988; Medam et al., 2016; Sidman et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Several researchers have proposed reversibility as a defining feature of symbolic reference.
source: Such reversibility is important because several researchers have proposed it as a defining feature of symbolic reference (Deacon, 1998; Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019; Nieder, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A limit of previous behavioural studies is that animals could have understood the reversibility of a symbolic relationship, but failed to express it behaviourally because of extraneous procedural or attentional factors.
source: Indeed, a limit of previous behavioural studies is that animals could have understood the reversibility of a symbolic relationship, but failed to express it behaviourally because of extraneous procedural or attentional factors, or because of a conflict between different brain processes (e.g. for maintaining the specific and rewarded learned pairing vs. generalising to the reverse order).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research methods.

claim: The current study used fMRI and a passive paradigm to directly probe whether any area of the monkey brain would exhibit surprise at a violation of the reversal of a learned association.
source: Here, we used fMRI and a passive paradigm to directly probe whether any area of the monkey brain would exhibit surprise at a violation of the reversal of a learned association.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study.

claim: There are occasional behavioural reports of spontaneous reversal of learned associations in one well-trained California sea lion and a Beluga whale.
source: Interpretation must remain cautious, as there are also some occasional behavioural reports of spontaneous reversal of learned associations, for instance in one well-trained California sea lion and a Beluga whale (Kastak et al., 2001; Murayama et al., 2017; Schusterman and Kastak, 1998) and possibly in 1 out of 20 baboons in Medam et al., 2016.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: With sufficient training, symbolic representation might eventually emerge in some animals.
source: These studies may indicate that, with sufficient training, symbolic representation might eventually emerge in some animals, as also suggested by the small reversal trend in a recent behaviour study in baboons (Chartier and Fagot, 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior research.

claim: Animals may begin to spontaneously reverse new associations once they have received extensive training with bidirectional ones.
source: However, they may also merely show that animals may begin to spontaneously reverse new associations once they have received extensive training with bidirectional ones (Kojima, 1984).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of prior research.

claim: The bulk of the literature strongly suggests that while animals easily learn indexical associations, they exhibit little or no evidence for genuine symbolic processing.
source: The bulk of the literature strongly suggests that while animals easily learn indexical associations, especially monkeys and chimpanzees (Diester and Nieder, 2007; Livingstone et al., 2010; Matsuzawa, 1985; Premack, 1971), but also dogs (Fugazza et al., 2021; Kaminski et al., 2004), vocal birds (e.g. Pepperberg, 2009), and even bees (Howard et al., 2019), they exhibit little or no evidence for genuine symbolic processing.
evidence: This is a summary of prior research supported by multiple citations.

claim: Discriminating symbolic from indexical representations can be achieved by testing for spontaneous reversibility between the labels and the objects, or by testing for the presence of systematic compositional relationships among the labels.
source: Discriminating symbolic from indexical representations can be achieved by testing for spontaneous reversibility between the labels and the objects, as in the current study, or by testing for the presence of systematic compositional relationships among the labels (Nieder, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about how to distinguish symbolic from indexical representations.

claim: One previous study showed preliminary evidence for a lack of reversibility in macaque monkey inferotemporal cortex, but only recorded on a subset of neurons, and after extensive training on pairs of visual images (816 exposures per pair).
source: One previous study showed preliminary evidence for a lack of reversibility in macaque monkey inferotemporal cortex (Meyer and Olson, 2011), but only recorded on a subset of neurons, and after extensive training on pairs of visual images (816 exposures per pair).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A similar set of arbitrary stimuli and extensive training protocol (258 trials per pair) was used in an fMRI study of stimulus association in humans, where congruity effects were also found to be restricted to early visual areas.
source: Interestingly, a similar set of arbitrary stimuli and extensive training protocol (258 trials per pair) was used in an fMRI study of stimulus association in humans, where congruity effects were also found to be restricted to early visual areas (Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Extensive training might have led to low-level and rigid encoding in the trained direction.
source: Such extensive training might have led to low-level and rigid encoding in the trained direction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior research findings.

claim: In the current study, in monkeys, just 24 exposures per pair were sufficient to observe a surprise effect in the canonical direction, yet without generalisation in the reverse direction, even after longer exposures.
source: It is therefore instructive that, here, in monkeys, we found irreversibility after a very short training period. Indeed, in experiment 2, just 24 exposures per pair were sufficient to observe a surprise effect in the canonical direction, yet without generalisation in the reverse direction, even after longer exposures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study.

claim: The current study strived to make the objects concrete and recognisable to the monkeys, while the labels were as abstract as possible to promote a symbol-referent asymmetry in the pairs.
source: In addition, we strived to make the objects concrete and recognisable to the monkeys (by using pictures of toys that were familiar to them, taken from various angles), while the labels were as abstract as possible to promote a symbol-referent asymmetry in the pairs.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design choices in the current study.

claim: The present animals had extensive experience with human speech.
source: Furthermore, the present animals had extensive experience with human speech.
evidence: This describes the background of the animals used in the study.

claim: Human preverbal infants easily learn labels in a lab setting and spontaneously reverse associations after only a short training period.
source: Finally, while the present lab setting could be judged artificial and not easily conducive to language acquisition, previous evidence indicates that human preverbal infants easily learn labels in such a setting (Mersad et al., 2021) and spontaneously reverse associations after only a short training period (Ekramnia and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019; Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Non-human primates are often considered the animal model of choice to understand the neural correlates of high-level cognitive functions in humans.
source: Non-human primates are often considered the animal model of choice to understand the neural correlates of high-level cognitive functions in humans (Feng et al., 2020; Newsome and Stein-Aviles, 1999; Roelfsema and Treue, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many studies have emphasised the similarity between human and non-human primates in terms of brain anatomy, physiology, and behaviour.
source: Accordingly, many studies have emphasised the similarity between human and non-human primates in terms of brain anatomy, physiology, and behaviour (Caspari et al., 2018; De Valois et al., 1974; Erb et al., 2019; Hackett et al., 2001; Harwerth and Smith, 1985; Mantini et al., 2012a; Mantini et al., 2012b; Mantini et al., 2011; Margulies et al., 2016; Petrides et al., 2012; Uhrig et al., 2014; Warren, 1974; Wilson et al., 2017; Wise, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Important differences between human and monkey brains have been reported.
source: At the same time, important differences between human and monkey brains have been reported as well (Passingham, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Using a direct comparison with fMRI, some specific functional differences have been found between humans and monkeys.
source: Using a direct comparison with fMRI, some specific functional differences have been found (Denys et al., 2004a; Denys et al., 2004b; Mantini et al., 2013; Vanduffel et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In contrast to humans, monkeys show clear feature tuning in the prefrontal cortex.
source: Particularly relevant is that, in contrast to humans, monkeys show clear feature tuning in the prefrontal cortex, which is in line with the sensory activation we found in monkey PFC (Figure 1C) and the involvement of monkey PFC in the congruity effect in experiment 2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Many anatomical differences have been reported between humans and monkeys using MRI as well as histological methods.
source: Many anatomical differences have been reported between humans and monkeys using MRI as well as histological methods.
evidence: This is a general statement about prior research.

claim: The human brain is exceptionally large.
source: In particular, the human brain is exceptionally large (Herculano-Houzel, 2012), and contains a number of structural differences compared to the brains of other primates (Chaplin et al., 2013; Leroy et al., 2015; Neubert et al., 2014; Palomero-Gallagher and Zilles, 2019; Rilling, 2014; Schenker et al., 2010; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The human arcuate fasciculus provides a strong direct connection between inferior prefrontal and temporal areas involved in language processing, while this bundle is reduced and does not extend as anteriorly and as ventrally in other primates, including chimpanzees.
source: Notably, while the human arcuate fasciculus provides a strong direct connection between inferior prefrontal and temporal areas involved in language processing, this bundle is reduced and does not extend as anteriorly and as ventrally in other primates, including chimpanzees (Balezeau et al., 2020; Eichert et al., 2020; Rilling et al., 2011; Rilling et al., 2008; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The PFC is selectively increased in terms of tissue volume in humans.
source: Also, the PFC is selectively increased in terms of tissue volume (Chaplin et al., 2013; Donahue et al., 2018; Hill et al., 2010; Smaers et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The selective increase in PFC tissue volume may not translate to a selective increase in terms of the number of PFC neurons.
source: While this may not translate to a selective increase in terms of the number of PFC neurons (Gabi et al., 2016), dendritic arborisations and synaptic density are larger in human PFC (Elston, 2007; Hilgetag and Goulas, 2020; Shibata et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dendritic arborisations and synaptic density are larger in human PFC.
source: While this may not translate to a selective increase in terms of the number of PFC neurons (Gabi et al., 2016), dendritic arborisations and synaptic density are larger in human PFC (Elston, 2007; Hilgetag and Goulas, 2020; Shibata et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Anatomical differences between humans and monkeys may underlie the fundamental differences in language learning abilities between these species, but this is still controversial.
source: These anatomical differences may underlie the fundamental differences in language learning abilities between these species, but this is still controversial (e.g. Hopkins et al., 2012; Iriki, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the relationship between anatomy and function, with citations to prior research.

claim: Reversibility of associations, a crucial element in the ability to attach symbols to objects and concepts, sharply differs between human and non-human primates.
source: Here, we show that reversibility of associations, a crucial element in the ability to attach symbols to objects and concepts, sharply differs between human and non-human primates and offers a more tractable way to investigate potential differences between species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study.

claim: The striking interspecies difference in size and extent of the violation effect as measured with fMRI points to a more efficient species-specific learning system.
source: The striking interspecies difference in size and extent of the violation effect as measured with fMRI, even for purely canonical stimuli, points to a more efficient species-specific learning system, that our experiment tentatively relates to a symbolic competence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study.

claim: The areas that specifically activated in humans when the reversed association was violated were not limited to the classical language network in the left hemisphere.
source: The areas that specifically activated in humans when the reversed association was violated were not limited to the classical language network in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study.

claim: The areas activated in humans extended bilaterally to homolog areas of the right hemisphere, which are involved for instance in the acquisition of musical languages.
source: They extended bilaterally to homolog areas of the right hemisphere, which are involved for instance in the acquisition of musical languages (Patel, 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by a citation.

claim: The areas activated in humans also extend dorsally to the MFG and IPS which are involved in the acquisition of the language of numbers, geometry and higher mathematics.
source: They also extend dorsally to the MFG and IPS which are involved in the acquisition of the language of numbers, geometry and higher mathematics (Amalric and Dehaene, 2016; Piazza, 2010; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by citations.

claim: An ROI analysis shows that the areas activated in humans also include the VWFA and vicinity.
source: Finally, an ROI analysis shows that they also include the VWFA and vicinity.
evidence: This is a finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: The VWFA is known to be sensitive to letters, but also to other visual symbols such as a new learned face-like script or emblematic pictures of famous cities.
source: The VWFA is known to be sensitive to letters, but also to other visual symbols such as a new learned face-like script (Moore et al., 2014) or emblematic pictures of famous cities (e.g. the Eiffel tower for Paris; Song et al., 2012), and the nearby lateral inferotemporal cortex responds to Arabic numerals and other mathematical symbols (Amalric and Dehaene, 2016; Shum et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The extended areas activated in humans correspond to regions whose cortical expansion and connectivity patterns are maximally different in humans compared to other primates.
source: Strikingly, these extended areas, shown in Figure 2, correspond to regions whose cortical expansion and connectivity patterns are maximally different in humans compared to other primates (Chaplin et al., 2013; Donahue et al., 2018; Hill et al., 2010; Smaers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: The extended areas activated in humans fit with a previous fMRI comparison of humans and macaque monkeys, where humans were shown to exhibit uniquely abstract and integrative representations of numerical and sequence patterns in these regions.
source: They also fit with a previous fMRI comparison of humans and macaque monkeys, where humans were shown to exhibit uniquely abstract and integrative representations of numerical and sequence patterns in these regions (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings and supported by a citation.

claim: The observed changes in humans are bilateral, extended, and go beyond the language network per se.
source: In all of these studies, the observed changes are bilateral, extended, and go beyond the language network per se.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the current study.

claim: The extended network does not fit with the hypothesis that a single localised system, such as natural language or a universal generative faculty, is the primary engine of all human-specific abstract symbolic abilities.
source: Such an extended network does not fit with the hypothesis that a single localised system, such as natural language or a universal generative faculty, is the primary engine of all human-specific abstract symbolic abilities (Hauser and Watumull, 2017; Spelke, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: The results suggest that multiple parallel and partially dissociable human brain networks possess symbolic abilities and deploy them in different domains such as natural language, music and mathematics.
source: Rather, our results suggest that multiple parallel and partially dissociable human brain networks possess symbolic abilities and deploy them in different domains such as natural language, music and mathematics (Amalric and Dehaene, 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Dehaene et al., 2022; Fedorenko et al., 2011; Fedorenko and Varley, 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Most learning rules, such as spike-time-dependent plasticity, are sensitive to temporal order and timing.
source: Interestingly, most learning rules, such as spike-time-dependent plasticity, are sensitive to temporal order and timing, a feature of fundamental importance for predictive coding.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Humans seem to forget the temporal order in which pairs of stimuli are presented when they store them at a symbolic level.
source: In contrast, as indicated by the behavioural results of experiment 2, humans seem to forget the temporal order in which pairs of stimuli are presented when they store them at a symbolic level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of experiment 2.

claim: Forgetting temporal order has been interpreted as improper causal reasoning.
source: This has been interpreted as improper causal reasoning (Ogawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal-dependent neuronal replay of sequences of events can occur in forward and reverse temporal order in both humans and non-human animals.
source: The most prominent candidate, in both humans and non-human animals, is hippocampal-dependent neuronal replay of sequences of events, which can occur in forward and reverse temporal order (Foster, 2017; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sequence reversal may be important during learning, in order to trace back to a memorised event that led to a reward.
source: Sequence reversal may be important during learning, in order to trace back to a memorised event that led to a reward.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the function of sequence reversal.

claim: A retroactive gradient has been shown in memory storage in humans, where memory is strongest for stimuli that were presented close to the reward but preceding it.
source: In line with this, a retroactive gradient has been shown in memory storage in humans, where memory is strongest for stimuli that were presented close to the reward but preceding it (Braun et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: This memory trace may explain the slight facilitation observed in baboons when they learn reversed congruent pairs relative to reversed incongruent pairs.
source: This memory trace may explain the slight facilitation observed in baboons when they learn reversed congruent pairs relative to reversed incongruent pairs (Chartier and Fagot, 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of prior research findings.

claim: Although neuronal replay in both forward and reverse directions exists in non-human animals, it might be that this mechanism has selectively expanded to symbol-related areas of the human brain.
source: Although neuronal replay in both forward and reverse directions exists in non-human animals, it might be that this mechanism has selectively expanded to symbol-related areas of the human brain – a clear hypothesis for future work.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis for future research.

claim: Even humans do not always disregard temporal order for all associations between stimulus pairs – for instance, they remember letters of the alphabet in a fixed temporal order.
source: Obviously, even humans do not always disregard temporal order for all associations between stimulus pairs – for instance, they remember letters of the alphabet in a fixed temporal order (Klahr et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the current study, the pairs comprised one fixed and abstract element (either linguistic or graphical), which served as a label, paired with several different views of a concrete object.
source: Here, the pairs comprised one fixed and abstract element (either linguistic or graphical), which served as a label, paired with several different views of a concrete object.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design in the current study.

claim: In human infants, the association of a label with the presentation of objects helps them construct the object category.
source: In human infants, the association of a label with the presentation of objects helps them construct the object category, as revealed by several experiments in which infants discriminate between categories (Ferry et al., 2013), or correctly process the number of objects (Xu et al., 2005) when the categories and objects are named, but not in the absence of a label.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Preverbal infants are flexible and accept pictures as labels for a rule, as well as monkey vocalisations and tones as labels for an animal category.
source: Interestingly, preverbal infants are flexible and accept pictures as labels for a rule (Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019), as well as monkey vocalisations and tones as labels for an animal category (Ferguson and Waxman, 2016; Ferry et al., 2013), whereas older infants who have been exposed to many social situations in which language is the primary symbolic medium to transfer information, expect symbolic labels to be in the native language (Perszyk and Waxman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Due to ethical and financial reasons, only 4 monkeys were tested, while 55 humans were tested in total.
source: First, due to ethical and financial reasons we only tested 4 monkeys, while we tested 55 humans in total.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current study.

claim: It is common in primate physiological studies to report the results for two animals, but this makes it challenging to extrapolate the results to the whole species.
source: While it is common in primate physiological studies to report the results for two animals, this makes it challenging to extrapolate the results to the whole species (Fries and Maris, 2022).
evidence: This is a methodological concern supported by a citation.

claim: To address the small sample size concern, the authors combined the results from two different labs, collecting data from two animals in each lab.
source: To address this point, we combined the results from two different labs, collecting data from two animals in each lab.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to address a limitation.

claim: The interspecies differences observed could be due to a number of hard-to-control factors, including a lifetime of open-field experiences and education in human adults.
source: A second limitation is that the interspecies differences that we observed could be due to a number of hard-to-control factors. While we ensured greater attention and motivation in experiment 2, other obvious differences include a lifetime of open-field experiences and education in our human adults, which was not available to monkeys and includes a strong bias towards explicit learning of symbolic systems (e.g. words, letters, digits, etc).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current study.

claim: The fact that 5-month-old infants, who lack extensive experience, also show a similar symbolic reversibility effect suggests that experiential factors may not fully explain the findings.
source: As noted above, however, the fact that 5-month-old infants, who lack such extensive experience, also show a similar symbolic reversibility effect (Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019) suggest that these factors may not fully explain our findings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior research to address a limitation.

claim: A large body of literature has shown that many non-human primates, including macaque monkeys, can make multi-modal associations between the faces and the vocalisations of individual animals they are familiar with.
source: A large body of literature has shown that many non-human primates, including macaque monkeys, can make multi-modal associations between the faces and the vocalisations of individual animals they are familiar with (Sliwa et al., 2011; Seyfarth and Cheney, 2015), although the training generally takes place with a simultaneous presentation of faces and vocalisations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Even if some specific circuits such as the identity recognition system were shown to exhibit a spontaneous reversal of associations in non-human primates, the human brain may still differ in its flexible ability to associate arbitrary symbols with any mental representation in a bidirectional manner.
source: Note however that, even if some specific circuits such as the identity recognition system were shown to exhibit a spontaneous reversal of associations in non-human primates, the human brain may still differ in its flexible ability to associate arbitrary symbols with any mental representation in a bidirectional manner, as studied here.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential differences between species.

claim: The distributed bilateral activation observed in areas of human prefrontal cortex and higher temporal and parietal cortices suggests that, during its recent evolution and expansion, the human workspace may have acquired a capacity to process arbitrary symbol systems.
source: The distributed bilateral activation observed here in areas of human prefrontal cortex and higher temporal and parietal cortices, which are thought to form a flexible global neuronal workspace (Mashour et al., 2020), suggests that, during its recent evolution and expansion, the human workspace may have acquired a capacity to process arbitrary symbol systems (Dehaene et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the current study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Testing non-human primates closer to humans, such as chimpanzees, might yield different conclusions.
source: Testing non-human primates closer to humans, such as chimpanzees, might yield different conclusions.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Reversible symbolic learning should also be evaluated in vocal learners such as songbirds and parrots, as some of them demonstrate sophisticated and flexible label learning.
source: Reversible symbolic learning should also be evaluated in vocal learners such as songbirds and parrots, as some of them demonstrate sophisticated and flexible label learning (see e.g. Pepperberg and Carey, 2012).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by a citation.

claim: In dogs, social interactions between the dog and the experimenter during learning facilitate associations.
source: Furthermore, in dogs, social interactions between the dog and the experimenter during learning facilitate associations (Fugazza et al., 2021), as is also the case in infants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There might be a critical period during which reversible symbolic representation might be possible with appropriate training procedures in monkeys.
source: Finally, we only tested adult monkeys, yet there might be a critical period during which reversible symbolic representation might be possible with appropriate training procedures; indeed, juvenile macaques learn better and faster to associate an arbitrary label with visual quantities than adults (Srihasam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research supported by a citation.

claim: The present work provides a simple experimental paradigm that can easily be extended to test whether humans are unique in their ability to acquire symbols.
source: The present work provides a simple experimental paradigm that can easily be extended to all these cases, thus offering a unique opportunity to test whether humans are unique in their ability to acquire symbols.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the current study's paradigm.
